records.title: Voluntary chin rest
records.summary:
Teach CHIN as a voluntary cooperative-care skill with clear stop signals.
The dog voluntarily places the underside of its chin on a still open hand or stable padded target, remains briefly, and can disengage without restraint.
records.body:
goal:
Teach CHIN as a voluntary cooperative-care skill with clear stop signals.

observable_target:
The dog voluntarily places the underside of its chin on a still open hand or stable padded target, remains briefly, and can disengage without restraint.

topics:
cooperative care
handling
husbandry
chin

aliases:
CHIN

eligibility:
Dog freely approaches the training area; no known unresolved pain or unsafe handling risk.
An adult can stop the exercise immediately and keep hands/equipment safely clear.

prerequisites:
Comfortable approach to the handler; no suspected neck, jaw or facial pain.
Reward marker already meaningful; an easy way to reset without pushing the head.
YES, GOOD and release meanings follow the current marker contract; do not introduce marker confusion during care.

contraindications:
Suspected pain, acute injury, unsafe aggression risk, or essential treatment that cannot be paused.
No use as a restraint method or a replacement for clinical care.

clarifying_questions:
What exact handling or equipment is difficult, and when did that change begin?
Any pain, injury, bite history or veterinary instructions?
Can the dog leave freely, and what does comfortable participation look like for this individual?
Is necessary care due before training can reasonably progress?

baseline_measurement:
Log the easiest voluntary response before any handling. Record context, target, cue used, response latency approximately, body movement, opt-outs and recovery; no diagnostic interpretation from a score alone.

setup:
Quiet secure room; non-slip surface; no children or other animals interrupting.
Handler positioned to the side; exit space remains available. Equipment begins at an easy distance.
Set one criterion before each repetition; plan how to stop and remove equipment before beginning.

equipment:
Stable non-slip floor and optional low padded target sized to the individual.
Small food rewards appropriate to the existing feeding plan.

welfare_checks:
Choose a target height that does not tilt the head back or load the neck. An open palm is a platform, not a clamp. Do not use a chin-rest cue during a procedure you cannot stop.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.
Food consumption and stillness alone do not demonstrate comfort. Observe willingness to re-enter and the whole body.

steps:
PRT-000201-S01
Discover the target: Sit or stand to the side without looming. Offer a stationary palm below natural chin height, leaving space to move away. Reward an orientation toward it initially, then a voluntary downward movement. Do not chase the muzzle with your hand.
Look for actual voluntary movement, not a head held still by contact.
Say YES at the selected approximation; withdraw the target and deliver the promised treat. Each YES ends that attempt.
Current step is comfortable and voluntary across easy repetitions; apply progression.advance before increasing difficulty.
Target unclear, repeated misses, slower re-entry or reduced willingness; use the easier preceding component.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.
PRT-000201-S02
Make brief contact: When approaches repeat, make the criterion one light chin contact. Keep fingers open. The head is supported only by what the dog chooses to place there; do not lift it into position.
A brief soft placement is sufficient; exclude mouth grabbing or a paw on the hand from the defined target.
YES at contact, then reward. Set the next invitation only after the dog has finished the treat.
Current step is comfortable and voluntary across easy repetitions; apply progression.advance before increasing difficulty.
Target unclear, repeated misses, slower re-entry or reduced willingness; use the easier preceding component.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.
PRT-000201-S03
Remove a food prompt: If an initial food prompt helped locate the target, first move the food to the other hand. Present the empty target before any food motion. If the dog searches for the lure, lower the criterion to a glance or approach, not a longer hold.
The target itself predicts the opportunity; food no longer has to be visible at the nose.
Mark the successful approximation with YES; bring the reward from its separate location afterward.
Current step is comfortable and voluntary across easy repetitions; apply progression.advance before increasing difficulty.
Target unclear, repeated misses, slower re-entry or reduced willingness; use the easier preceding component.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.
PRT-000201-S04
Add the cue: Once the offered target reliably produces contact, say CHIN once just before presenting it. Keep that order. After several easy pairings, reduce the size of the target presentation if helpful; the support surface still remains available.
Record whether the dog initiates before further prompting; do not chant the cue.
YES for the completed easy contact. A missed cue receives a pause and easier setup, not repeated commands.
Current step is comfortable and voluntary across easy repetitions; apply progression.advance before increasing difficulty.
Target unclear, repeated misses, slower re-entry or reduced willingness; use the easier preceding component.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.
PRT-000201-S05
Add tiny duration: Begin with the already easy contact. On a later repetition delay the terminal marker for a very small interval. If GOOD is already understood, use it while the chin remains placed, then soon say YES and treat.
Chin remains supported by choice; neck stays comfortable and the dog can leave.
GOOD means continue with reward later, never release. YES releases and earns the treat; OKAY is a general release without a promised treat.
Current step is comfortable and voluntary across easy repetitions; apply progression.advance before increasing difficulty.
Target unclear, repeated misses, slower re-entry or reduced willingness; use the easier preceding component.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.
PRT-000201-S06
Introduce a simulated care event: Only after the rest itself is comfortable, move an empty second hand a small distance toward a non-sensitive shoulder area. End the movement before asking for more duration. Add an actual brief touch on a different, easier repetition only if appropriate.
If the chin lifts, immediately stop the approach or touch. Do not replace the chin or block retreat.
Reward successful short participation with YES. An opt-out is respected without NO or NOPE; invite again only if the dog freely returns.
Current step is comfortable and voluntary across easy repetitions; apply progression.advance before increasing difficulty.
Target unclear, repeated misses, slower re-entry or reduced willingness; use the easier preceding component.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.

session_plan:
Begin with one to three easy opportunities, then offer a break and reassess. This is an editable planning example, not a mandatory dose. End earlier whenever needed.
The goal is repeated comfortable participation, not finishing a body part, device fitting or fixed number of minutes.
Reduce target height, standing demands, reach or duration for the individual with appropriate professional advice. Never withhold needed care while waiting for training.

progression:
Repeat at the same easy level until re-entry is voluntary, movement remains comfortable and the target is predictable across separate short sessions. Change only one criterion. A suggested logging rule is four comfortable successes out of five across two mini-sessions; this is an editorial aid, not a validated threshold, and any concern overrides the count.
Repeat the same criterion only while the dog remains comfortable and freely re-engages. Record success without automatically adding difficulty.
Reduce reach, contact, duration or equipment proximity to the last comfortable version. Do not repeat the harder test to prove the dog can do it. If easy repetitions no longer look comfortable, finish rather than escalating rewards or restraint.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.
Veterinary assessment for pain, new handling changes, injury or clinical care needs. Qualified reward-based behavior support for persistent fear, defensive behavior or stalled acclimation; individualized risk plan for bite history.

troubleshooting:
Dog lifts the head as the second hand moves
The motion may be too difficult or predict handling.
Return to chin rest alone; make second-hand movement smaller or farther away.
Holding the jaw down or delaying release to finish the touch.
Dog mouths the target hand
Reward placement or target height may be confusing; discomfort is also possible.
Keep food separate, change target surface if suitable, and reward a smaller calm approach.
Closing the hand over the muzzle or treating mouth grabbing as defiance.

generalization:
Change only one element: room, familiar adult, target position or equipment. Return to the easiest acquisition step for that element. A home success does not certify performance at a clinic, groomer, crowded venue or during pain. Tell the next handler the exact cue and stop rule.

maintenance:
Include occasional easy rehearsal without a procedure. Keep the same words and consent boundary. Review after illness, injury, growth, equipment change or a bad experience. Do not test endurance to see whether the behavior is still trained.

limitations:
Original editorial training proposal; not clinically or behaviorally validated.
No guarantee of comfort, bite prevention, procedure tolerance or timeline.
No forced restraint, clipping technique, medication, sedation, or veterinary treatment instructions.

records.title: Voluntary paw presentation
records.summary:
Teach PAW as a voluntary cooperative-care skill with clear stop signals.
The dog chooses to place a front paw on a low open palm and can withdraw it without grip or resistance.
records.body:
goal:
Teach PAW as a voluntary cooperative-care skill with clear stop signals.

observable_target:
The dog chooses to place a front paw on a low open palm and can withdraw it without grip or resistance.

topics:
cooperative care
handling
husbandry
paw

aliases:
PAW

eligibility:
Dog freely approaches the training area; no known unresolved pain or unsafe handling risk.
An adult can stop the exercise immediately and keep hands/equipment safely clear.

prerequisites:
No lameness, sore pads, damaged nails or suspected joint pain.
Comfortable standing or sitting on the chosen surface without forced posture.
YES, GOOD and release meanings follow the current marker contract; do not introduce marker confusion during care.

contraindications:
Suspected pain, acute injury, unsafe aggression risk, or essential treatment that cannot be paused.
No use as a restraint method or a replacement for clinical care.

What exact handling or equipment is difficult, and when did that change begin?
Any pain, injury, bite history or veterinary instructions?

baseline_measurement:
Log the easiest voluntary response before any handling. Record context, target, cue used, response latency approximately, body movement, opt-outs and recovery; no diagnostic interpretation from a score alone.

setup:
Quiet secure room; non-slip surface; no children or other animals interrupting.
Handler positioned to the side; exit space remains available. Equipment begins at an easy distance.
Set one criterion before each repetition; plan how to stop and remove equipment before beginning.

equipment:
Non-slip floor; low open hand target; food rewards.
No nail tools in the initial skill sessions.

welfare_checks:
Keep the paw close to its natural supported position. Do not pull the leg forward, twist the wrist or suspend the dog by the limb. This front-paw exercise is not a rear-leg handling instruction.

Food consumption and stillness alone do not demonstrate comfort. Observe willingness to re-enter and the whole body.

steps:
PRT-000202-S01
Establish a balanced starting picture: Choose the posture the dog offers comfortably. Put an open hand low beside one front paw without touching or lifting it. Reward a small voluntary weight shift or paw movement toward the hand.
Three other limbs and the body remain balanced; the handler does not create the movement by pressure.
YES for the chosen approximation, treat, then remove the hand for a reset.
Current step is comfortable and voluntary across easy repetitions; apply progression.advance before increasing difficulty.
Target unclear, repeated misses, slower re-entry or reduced willingness; use the easier preceding component.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.
PRT-000202-S02
Capture contact: Offer the same low hand. As voluntary movements become predictable, reward a paw touching it. Do not scrape or tap the leg to make the paw lift. If contact is not offered, return to a smaller movement target.
The paw lands briefly on the hand rather than being scooped from the floor.
YES at contact; allow withdrawal and deliver the reward.
Current step is comfortable and voluntary across easy repetitions; apply progression.advance before increasing difficulty.
Target unclear, repeated misses, slower re-entry or reduced willingness; use the easier preceding component.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.
PRT-000202-S03
Separate food from the target: If food in a closed hand started pawing, move food elsewhere and use an open palm promptly. Reward one gentle touch rather than repeated scratching. Stop if the exercise becomes frantic.
The dog selects the palm without smelling food inside it.
Treat follows YES from the other hand or pouch. Do not keep bait hidden in the target palm indefinitely.
Current step is comfortable and voluntary across easy repetitions; apply progression.advance before increasing difficulty.
Target unclear, repeated misses, slower re-entry or reduced willingness; use the easier preceding component.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.
PRT-000202-S04
Name the offered action: Say PAW once immediately before the familiar empty-palm invitation when the response is already likely. Keep the same side initially; name different sides only after the first skill is clear.
Measure whether the dog offers the trained paw without lifting assistance.
YES for a voluntary presentation. Misses lead to an easier hand position or a break.
Current step is comfortable and voluntary across easy repetitions; apply progression.advance before increasing difficulty.
Target unclear, repeated misses, slower re-entry or reduced willingness; use the easier preceding component.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.
PRT-000202-S05
Develop support without gripping: Initially the hand simply receives the paw. Later allow a tiny interval before release. Keep fingers open and support lightly from below without squeezing. Do not add inspection at the same time.
The dog remains balanced and can take the paw back at any moment.
GOOD may bridge an already easy short hold; YES then releases and earns a treat. Give OKAY if ending without a food promise.
Current step is comfortable and voluntary across easy repetitions; apply progression.advance before increasing difficulty.
Target unclear, repeated misses, slower re-entry or reduced willingness; use the easier preceding component.
Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.
PRT-000202-S06
Generalize carefully: Practice the other front paw as a new lesson, then a familiar second adult at the easiest contact stage. Add a moment of looking at the paw only after voluntary support remains comfortable.
Different sides, people and surfaces may have different baselines.
Keep rewards generous during a new context. The paw being withdrawn ends contact immediately, regardless of the planned marker.

Pause immediately for withdrawal, freezing, avoidance, escalating tension, growling, snapping, suspected pain or loss of balance. Remove the training demand without grabbing or pursuit. Seek professional help for fear/aggression; suspected injury needs veterinary assessment.

The goal is repeated comfortable participation, not finishing a body part, device fitting or fixed number of minutes.
Reduce target height, standing demands, reach or duration for the individual with appropriate professional advice. Never withhold needed care while waiting for training.

Veterinary assessment for pain, new handling changes, injury or clinical care needs. Qualified reward-based behavior support for persistent fear, defensive behavior or stalled acclimation; individualized risk plan for bite history.

troubleshooting:
Dog scratches repeatedly
The criterion or reward placement may encourage repeated pawing.
Mark the first light contact earlier and reset before scratching starts.
Holding the paw to prevent scratching.
Dog refuses only one paw
Pain, balance differences or learning history are possible.
Stop comparing sides and seek veterinary assessment for new asymmetry or discomfort.
Forcing the reluctant limb because the other side was easy.

Change only one element: room, familiar adult, target position or equipment. Return to the easiest acquisition step for that element. A home success does not certify performance at a clinic, groomer, crowded venue or during pain. Tell the next handler the exact cue and stop rule.

records.title: Polite greetings: four feet on the floor
records.summary:
Build a greeting that is comfortable for both dog and visitor; contact is optional, not owed.
Log grounded approaches, voluntary contacts and jumping attempts. Add only one change: helper movement, new adult or entrance location. Progress when the dog repeatedly succeeds with loose comfortable movement, not just physical suppression.

observable_target:

topics:
training
behavior_household
SCA-BH-001

aliases:
jumping up
greet visitors
four on floor

eligibility:
Voluntary comfortable beginner practice in a secure low-distraction setting; professional review before public use

prerequisites:
Dog can comfortably notice a familiar adult without threatening, hiding or frantic pulling. Fearful greetings belong in the confidence module instead.
Handler can control access with a secure barrier without restraining the dog against a visitor. Use an adult helper, not a child or frail visitor.

contraindications:
Growling, freezing, hiding, escape attempts, painful sitting, escalating mouthing or any fall/bite risk: stop contact and obtain appropriate veterinary/behavior help.

clarifying_questions:
What happens immediately before and after the behavior?
When did it begin, and is there pain, illness, fear, guarding or a bite history?
Who shares the setting and can safe separation be maintained?

baseline_measurement:
Record context, observable behavior, management in place, comfort and recovery; do not provoke behavior to collect baseline data.

setup:
Decide the actual target: four feet grounded is enough; a sit is optional if comfortable and already understood.
Brief the helper before bringing out the dog. Agree on a stop signal and a retreat route. Put rewards where they can be delivered low without reaching over the head.
Record which people, entrances and movements cause jumping. Begin away from the busy front door.

equipment:
Secure appropriate barriers
Comfortable individual equipment where needed
Suitable familiar reward if used
Observation log

welfare_checks:
Allow safe retreat and ordinary rest, food, water and toileting needs.
Stop for fear, pain, unsafe proximity or loss of safe management.

SCA-BH-001-S1
Begin with the helper stationary at a distance where the dog remains comfortable. Before a jump occurs, mark an observed four-feet moment with YES and deliver the promised treat low beside the handler. This releases the trial; it does not require a continuing sit.
Observe action-specific behavior and whole-dog comfort; absence of movement or vocalization does not prove comfort.
YES releases the current position/task and promises a treat; GOOD means continue holding with reward later. NO stops unwanted behavior; NOPE is playful-teaching retry feedback, not a fear or aggression intervention. OKAY is general release. Positional cues imply holding until release or another command. These definitions do not authorize physical corrections.
Log grounded approaches, voluntary contacts and jumping attempts. Add only one change: helper movement, new adult or entrance location. Progress when the dog repeatedly succeeds with loose comfortable movement, not just physical suppression.
If jumping repeats, shorten the interaction or increase distance before the next trial. If the dog cannot settle at that setup, end greetings and use comfortable separation rather than repeat failures.
Growling, freezing, hiding, escape attempts, painful sitting, escalating mouthing or any fall/bite risk: stop contact and obtain appropriate veterinary/behavior help.

setup:

records.title: Shared households: multi-dog routines and child safety
records.summary:
Organize human supervision and physical separation so ordinary routines do not depend on dogs tolerating pressure or children reading subtle signals.
Measure adult adherence, secure transitions and each dog’s voluntary access to rest, not how much rough handling a dog tolerates. Add complexity only where the adults can maintain the safety plan.

goal:
Organize human supervision and physical separation so ordinary routines do not depend on dogs tolerating pressure or children reading subtle signals.

observable_target:
Measure adult adherence, secure transitions and each dog’s voluntary access to rest, not how much rough handling a dog tolerates. Add complexity only where the adults can maintain the safety plan.

topics:
training
behavior_household
SCA-BH-008

aliases:
children dogs
multi dog home
household safety
dog dog conflict

eligibility:
Voluntary comfortable beginner practice in a secure low-distraction setting; professional review before public use

prerequisites:
An adult must be responsible for management; a child is never the safety monitor.
Assess each dog individually, prior conflicts, mobility, hearing/vision, guarding and ability to rest behind barriers. A peaceful past is not a guarantee.

contraindications:
Growling toward a child, stalking or chasing vulnerable household members, bites, inter-dog injury, blocked access to necessities or management that adults cannot maintain requires prompt professional assessment and reliable separation.

clarifying_questions:
What happens immediately before and after the behavior?
When did it begin, and is there pain, illness, fear, guarding or a bite history?
Who shares the setting and can safe separation be maintained?

baseline_measurement:
Record context, observable behavior, management in place, comfort and recovery; do not provoke behavior to collect baseline data.

setup:
Draw a simple zone map: child play area, dog rest area, feeding areas, doorway traffic and safe adult-controlled transitions.
Use separation whenever an adult cannot actively supervise. Presence in the same room while distracted is not reliable monitoring. Check barrier height, reach-through gaps and latch access.
Give each dog safe access to water, rest and needed care. Duplicating bowls is not enough if one dog blocks the other’s route.

equipment:
Secure appropriate barriers
Comfortable individual equipment where needed
Suitable familiar reward if used
Observation log

welfare_checks:
Allow safe retreat and ordinary rest, food, water and toileting needs.
Stop for fear, pain, unsafe proximity or loss of safe management.

prerequisites:

clarifying_questions:

baseline_measurement:

setup:

welfare_checks:

records.body:
goal:
Build easy re-engagement and an optional brief attention cue without forcing eye contact.

observable_target:
Editorial target: several voluntary returns plus four of five brief cued orientations at the current prompt level. Increase only one dimension; comfort outranks duration.

topics:
training
core_cues
SCA-CUE-113

aliases:
Voluntary engagement and optional Watch

eligibility:
Voluntary comfortable beginner practice in a secure low-distraction setting; professional review before public use

prerequisites:
Comfortable voluntary orientation and ability to read disengagement.

contraindications:
Accept a less intense orientation when direct gaze is uncomfortable. Do not use attention to suppress vigilance in unsafe situations.

clarifying_questions:
Has the behavior been taught in this setting?
Any pain, distress, guarding, bite history or recent change?
What cue, marker, prompt and reward are currently used?

baseline_measurement:
Record current prompt level, attempts/successes, response latency, hold seconds, handler distance, distraction and comfort. Do not infer intention.

setup:
Choose orientation toward the face or upper body; direct staring is unnecessary. Decide whether a separate Watch cue is useful or spontaneous check-ins suffice.

equipment:
Secure quiet space
Suitable familiar reward
Comfortable non-slip surface
Practice log

welfare_checks:
Maintain access to ordinary needs; no deprivation to obtain performance.
Observe whole-dog comfort; stop for pain, distress, freezing, escape attempts or unsafe handling.

Stand without looming and wait for a voluntary orientation. Say YES and deliver a treat; allow the dog to look around again.

records.title: Touch: voluntary nose-to-hand targeting
records.summary:
The dog voluntarily touches an offered hand with the nose.
Proposed target: four of five nose contacts to an unscented stationary hand in two short sessions, then one small position change. Track nose versus paw or mouth contact.
records.body:
goal:
The dog voluntarily touches an offered hand with the nose.

observable_target:
Proposed target: four of five nose contacts to an unscented stationary hand in two short sessions, then one small position change. Track nose versus paw or mouth contact.

topics:
training
core_cues
SCA-CUE-114

aliases:
Touch: voluntary nose-to-hand targeting

eligibility:
Voluntary comfortable beginner practice in a secure low-distraction setting; professional review before public use

prerequisites:
Safe hand proximity, comfortable food delivery, no guarding or biting risk in this setup.

contraindications:
Touch is not consent to examination or grooming. Unsafe hand behavior requires an individualized plan.

clarifying_questions:
Has the behavior been taught in this setting?
Any pain, distress, guarding, bite history or recent change?
What cue, marker, prompt and reward are currently used?

baseline_measurement:
Record current prompt level, attempts/successes, response latency, hold seconds, handler distance, distraction and comfort. Do not infer intention.

setup:
Present a still open palm or two fingers near nose height. Keep food in the other hand. Do not push fingers into the face or mouth.

equipment:
Secure quiet space
Suitable familiar reward
Comfortable non-slip surface
Practice log

welfare_checks:
Maintain access to ordinary needs; no deprivation to obtain performance.
Observe whole-dog comfort; stop for pain, distress, freezing, escape attempts or unsafe handling.

Comfortable demonstrated understanding of the step, using the module progression before increasing demands.
Mouthing, pawing, flinching or backing away: pause, lower excitement and revise presentation. Do not hold the hand against the nose.
Touch is not consent to examination or grooming. Unsafe hand behavior requires an individualized plan.

records.summary:
The dog stands voluntarily and holds only the taught attainable interval.
Draft target: four of five voluntary stands at the current prompt level, then a brief still hold. Track extra steps separately; change surface and duration independently.
records.body:

Voluntary comfortable beginner practice in a secure low-distraction setting; professional review before public use

contraindications:

Secure quiet space
Suitable familiar reward
Comfortable non-slip surface
Practice log

Maintain access to ordinary needs; no deprivation to obtain performance.

records.title: Heel: side-position precision versus loose leash
records.summary:
Teach a short defined side-position task distinct from ordinary loose-leash exploration.
Proposed target: four of five side entries, followed by several brief slack-leash segments at the defined alignment. Increase steps, turns or distraction separately.

goal:

aliases:

eligibility:
Voluntary comfortable beginner practice in a secure low-distraction setting; professional review before public use

prerequisites:

contraindications:
No precision drills at traffic edges. Adapt for handler mobility and dog comfort; use secure management independent of obedience.

Practice log

records.title: Retrieve / fetch / bring: a voluntary safe-object chain
records.summary:
Pick up one familiar safe object, carry it a short distance to the handler, and voluntarily deliver it; this is a recreational retrieve, not a forced hold or a service task.
Editor-proposed example: four comfortable complete chains in five easy opportunities over two short sessions before adding one small distance change. Track pickup, carry, arrival and release separately; four pickups alone do not meet the chain criterion.
records.body:
goal:
Pick up one familiar safe object, carry it a short distance to the handler, and voluntarily deliver it; this is a recreational retrieve, not a forced hold or a service task.

observable_target:
Editor-proposed example: four comfortable complete chains in five easy opportunities over two short sessions before adding one small distance change. Track pickup, carry, arrival and release separately; four pickups alone do not meet the chain criterion.

topics:
training
optional_advanced_skills
SCA-ADV-001

aliases:
Retrieve / fetch / bring

eligibility:
Voluntary comfortable individual practice; physical suitability and qualified review required before public use.

prerequisites:
Comfortable supervised object interaction, a voluntary trade/drop skill, and a short secure recall are separate prerequisites.
No current guarding, swallowing attempts, painful chewing, or conflict around taking objects.

contraindications:
No forced mouth opening, holding the muzzle shut, ear/toe pressure, repeated throws to exhaustion, or taking a guarded object.
Do not use valuable household items, medication containers, or objects with detachable parts.

clarifying_questions:
Has the behavior been taught in this setting?
Any pain, distress, guarding, bite history or recent change?
What cue, marker, prompt and reward are currently used?

baseline_measurement:
Record comfortable baseline, exact approximation, prompt level, success and context before progression.

setup:
Begin within easy reaching distance in a quiet enclosed room. Put away competing toys and remove children or other dogs.
Define delivery as release over a low open hand or a broad shallow tray. A tray can reduce pressure from reaching toward the mouth.

equipment:
One intact purpose-made dog toy too large to swallow and comfortable to carry; inspect before every session.
Open nonslip floor, small suitable treats, and a second familiar toy for optional swaps. No sticks, bones, sharp items, or hard small balls.

welfare_checks:
Use brief voluntary practice, often only a handful of easy attempts, with breaks and ordinary needs met. Session length follows this dog’s comfort rather than a compulsory clock. Stop for pain, limping, stiffness, repeated slipping, unusual breathing, freezing, escape attempts, escalating frustration, guarding or loss of voluntary participation. Sudden movement or behavior changes merit veterinary assessment; fear, guarding or unsafe handling merits qualified behavior/training support. Do not force posture or use restraint, deprivation or escalating pressure to obtain a trick.

steps:
SCA-ADV-001-S1
Build voluntary delivery first. Offer a familiar toy without pushing it into the mouth. If the dog chooses to hold it, present the previously taught drop/trade opportunity over the tray. Mark YES only after release; give the promised treat.
The dog can disengage freely and releases without prying or chasing. If possession causes tension, stop the chain and seek suitable help.
YES permits leaving the current target/position and promises a treat. GOOD means continue holding position; reward comes later. NO stops unwanted behavior; it does not authorize physical correction. NOPE is optional familiar playful retry feedback, not a harsh reprimand. OKAY is the general release. Positional cues imply holding until release or another command; a moving action has the explicitly taught endpoint. Do not terminal-mark an intermediate step and then demand the remainder of a chain.
Editor-proposed example: four comfortable complete chains in five easy opportunities over two short sessions before adding one small distance change. Track pickup, carry, arrival and release separately; four pickups alone do not meet the chain criterion.

records.title: Find it: recreational nosework and food-search games
records.summary:
Voluntarily search a small safe area for accessible familiar food or a toy; this is enrichment, not medical, operational, or certified scent detection.
Editor-proposed gate: several easy voluntary finds with relaxed continued participation before one slightly less visible hide. Log time to engagement and whether help was needed; speed is not the goal. There is no scent-detection accuracy certification in this game.

Walk once around a stable safe floor-level object and return toward the handler on a clear route.

observable_target:
Editor-proposed gate: four comfortable single loops in five easy opportunities across two sessions before a small handler-distance increase. Track full path, safe clearance, return and prompt level; speed does not count as improvement.

topics:
training
optional_advanced_skills
SCA-ADV-008

aliases:
Go around

eligibility:
Voluntary comfortable individual practice; physical suitability and qualified review required before public use.

prerequisites:
Comfortable following a hand target and an easy contained recall or approach.
Dog can walk broad curves without discomfort.

contraindications:
No leash entanglement, narrow turns, unstable furniture, public obstacles, or speed drills.

clarifying_questions:
Has the behavior been taught in this setting?
Any pain, distress, guarding, bite history or recent change?
What cue, marker, prompt and reward are currently used?

baseline_measurement:
Record comfortable baseline, exact approximation, prompt level, success and context before progression.

setup:
Inspect the entire route, not just the visible front. Keep enough space that neither the dog nor handler squeezes between the object and wall.
Choose a direction initially. Stand close enough to show a short simple arc without leaning over the dog.

equipment:
A broad stable smooth object without protrusions, loose fabric, sharp edges or a tipping risk; nonslip clear floor and treats.
Avoid trees with unsafe debris, light chairs, folding furniture, poles with guy lines, or items the dog may jump onto.

welfare_checks:
Use brief voluntary practice, often only a handful of easy attempts, with breaks and ordinary needs met. Session length follows this dog’s comfort rather than a compulsory clock. Stop for pain, limping, stiffness, repeated slipping, unusual breathing, freezing, escape attempts, escalating frustration, guarding or loss of voluntary participation. Sudden movement or behavior changes merit veterinary assessment; fear, guarding or unsafe handling merits qualified behavior/training support. Do not force posture or use restraint, deprivation or escalating pressure to obtain a trick.

steps:
step_id: SCA-ADV-008-S1
handler_action: Invite one or two steps beside the object with a familiar hand target. YES after this small comfortable segment and reward away from the object.
observe: The object is a visual route landmark, never a barrier used to trap the dog.
feedback_plan: YES permits leaving the current target/position and promises a treat. GOOD means continue holding position; reward comes later. NO stops unwanted behavior; it does not authorize physical correction. NOPE is optional familiar playful retry feedback, not a harsh reprimand. OKAY is the general release. Positional cues imply holding until release or another command; a moving action has the explicitly taught endpoint. Do not terminal-mark an intermediate step and then demand the remainder of a chain.
advance_if: Editor-proposed gate: four comfortable single loops in five easy opportunities across two sessions before a small handler-distance increase. Track full path, safe clearance, return and prompt level; speed does not count as improvement.
regress_if: Simplify the current target, restore a clear prompt or return to the last comfortable successful setup.
stop_if: Use brief voluntary practice, often only a handful of easy attempts, with breaks and ordinary needs met. Session length follows this dog’s comfort rather than a compulsory clock. Sudden movement or behavior changes merit veterinary assessment; fear, guarding or unsafe handling merits qualified behavior/training support. Do not force posture or use restraint, deprivation or escalating pressure to obtain a trick.

records.title: Under / through: easy open obstacle routes
records.summary:
Walk voluntarily through a wide open passage or beneath a high-clearance fixed structure without crouching, crawling, jumping, or feeling trapped.
Editor-proposed gate: several comfortable full crossings with normal gait and free exits before reducing a prompt or changing approach. Hesitation, low posture, abrupt retreat or rushing calls for an easier setup, not more pressure.

records.title: Paws up: front paws on a stable low platform
records.summary:
Voluntarily place both front paws on a broad stable low surface, hold briefly in comfort and return all paws to the floor on a clear exit cue; no climbing or balance challenge.
Editor-proposed gate: several easy voluntary two-paw placements and comfortable exits before reducing a prompt or adding a very short hold. Step quality and ability to exit matter more than counts. Higher platforms are not the next progression.

Create a positively learned place to remain briefly without using the station as restraint or punishment.
Draft target: four of five voluntary entries at the current distance, then several comfortable short holds ending with release. Increase seconds before minutes; extend only one difficulty dimension at a time.
records.body:
goal:
Create a positively learned place to remain briefly without using the station as restraint or punishment.

observable_target:
Draft target: four of five voluntary entries at the current distance, then several comfortable short holds ending with release. Increase seconds before minutes; extend only one difficulty dimension at a time.

topics:
training
foundations
SCA-TR-006

aliases:
Teach a station: entry first, duration second

eligibility:
Voluntary comfortable beginner practice in a secure low-distraction setting; professional review before public use

prerequisites:
Marker and release understanding; comfortable movement.
A stable, accessible station large enough for the dog. Basic position practice helps but is not a reason to force a posture.

contraindications:
Use gates or separate safe rooms for risky guest or child interactions; a place cue is not a substitute for separation.
Guarding the bed, growling when approached or unsafe handling needs professional assessment.
Adapt bed height and surface to the dog's physical ability.

clarifying_questions:
Has the behavior been taught in this setting?
Any pain, distress, guarding, bite history or recent change?
What cue, marker, prompt and reward are currently used?

baseline_measurement:
Record current prompt level, attempts/successes, response latency, hold seconds, handler distance, distraction and comfort. Do not infer intention.

setup:
Choose a non-slip mat or low accessible bed away from doors and busy traffic.
For the completed entry, define four paws within the boundary. Early shaping may reward smaller approaches, labeled as intermediate steps.
Begin without guests, children approaching or competing animals.

equipment:
Secure quiet space
Suitable familiar reward
Comfortable non-slip surface
Practice log

welfare_checks:
Maintain access to ordinary needs; no deprivation to obtain performance.
Observe whole-dog comfort; stop for pain, distress, freezing, escape attempts or unsafe handling.

steps:
SCA-TR-006-S1
Start near the station. Encourage voluntary exploration with a small lure or reward placement; do not drag the dog onto it.
Record the behavior specified in the action and whether participation remains comfortable.

Leaving repeatedly, reluctance to approach or growing vigilance means simplify or stop. Return to entry work if the boundary itself is unclear. Do not tether or physically pin the dog to make the duration happen.
Pain, distress, unsafe interaction or escalating handler frustration.

session_plan:
Short practice, often a few repetitions; source-informed 2–5 minute planning range where appropriate, not a mandatory duration.
Preserve engagement and clear feedback; avoid fatigue-based drilling.
Shorten or adapt for age, mobility, comfort, environment and individual response; no fixed completion deadline.

progression:
Draft target: four of five voluntary entries at the current distance, then several comfortable short holds ending with release. Increase seconds before minutes; extend only one difficulty dimension at a time.
Repeat current easy level if comfortable but inconsistent; do not simultaneously increase demands.

Stop for pain, distress, unsafe behavior or handler frustration.

troubleshooting:
She leaves immediately after YES.
Context, comfort, prompt history or communication may differ; question text alone does not establish cause.
That is consistent with YES: leaving is permitted and a treat follows. Teach a separate short hold with GOOD, then after the planned interval YES and the treat.
Expecting a 30-minute hold with guests after a few entry repetitions. Calling the station an off-switch and overlooking emotional distress. Using it only after unwanted behavior. Leaving a leash attached and unattended where entanglement is possible.
Can I use Place while visitors pet him?
Context, comfort, prompt history or communication may differ; question text alone does not establish cause.
Not as a way to require tolerance. Keep visitors from approaching if the dog is uncomfortable and use safe separation instead.
Expecting a 30-minute hold with guests after a few entry repetitions. Calling the station an off-switch and overlooking emotional distress. Using it only after unwanted behavior. Leaving a leash attached and unattended where entanglement is possible.

generalization:
Lower difficulty when changing location; vary duration, distance or distraction separately and maintain secure management.

maintenance:
Revisit short comfortable practice in the contexts needed; record regressions and adjust rather than assume permanent mastery.

limitations:
First beginner batch only; not complete training, diet or care coverage.
Numeric criteria are editorial proposals, not validated source-derived benchmarks.
No current deployed corpus match or clinical/professional validation.
No automatic advanced tool or correction instructions.

session_plan:
dose: Short practice, often a few repetitions; source-informed 2–5 minute planning range where appropriate, not a mandatory duration.
rationale: Preserve engagement and clear feedback; avoid fatigue-based drilling.
individual_adjustments: Shorten or adapt for age, mobility, comfort, environment and individual response; no fixed completion deadline.

progression:
advance: Draft target: around four of five comfortable successes at each recorded step across two sessions before increasing it. Reliability claims remain specific to tested conditions. These thresholds are editorial teaching defaults, not guarantees.
repeat: Repeat current easy level if comfortable but inconsistent; do not simultaneously increase demands.
regress: A worsening response, repeated errors, fatigue or distress means decrease demand or stop. A known skill can still fail because the setting exceeds current training; failure does not prove defiance.
stop: Stop for pain, distress, unsafe behavior or handler frustration.
refer: Aggression, resource guarding, panic or bite risk is not a routine proofing challenge; use safe separation and qualified support. observed_problem: He can hold for ten seconds inside. Can I try a minute in the park?
possible_explanations: Context, comfort, prompt history or communication may differ; question text alone does not establish cause.
next_action: That changes both duration and environment substantially. Start much easier in a quiet new location and rebuild from observed success.

observed_problem: Should I keep the same standard even if she is frightened?
possible_explanations: Context, comfort, prompt history or communication may differ; question text alone does not establish cause.
next_action: No. Safety and comfort come first. Create distance or leave, then reconsider the training plan rather than insisting on performance.

Lower difficulty when changing location; vary duration, distance or distraction separately and maintain secure management.

maintenance:
Revisit short comfortable practice in the contexts needed; record regressions and adjust rather than assume permanent mastery.

First beginner batch only; not complete training, diet or care coverage.
Numeric criteria are editorial proposals, not validated source-derived benchmarks.
No current deployed corpus match or clinical/professional validation.
No automatic advanced tool or correction instructions.

records.body: # Supreme Canine Academy — Canine care and life-stage planning Private review draft • 2026-11-01 • General education, observation and veterinary referral support, not diagnosis, treatment or a validated clinical resource. Seven modules supplement the training and nutrition collections; they do not replace either. Original planning worksheets below are editorial proposals, not tested clinical instruments. Source identities and claim provenance are maintained separately. **Training language throughout:** YES ends the position and promises a treat; GOOD means remain in position with reward later; NO means stop unwanted behavior; NOPE means adjust an incorrect playful teaching attempt; OKAY is general release. Positional commands imply holding until release or another command. Pain, fear, illness, exhaustion and urgent care are not obedience failures. Never use this cue system to compel a distressed dog to tolerate care. ## EDU-000501 — Puppy development and safe social exposure ### Purpose and evidence boundary Early positive social experiences matter; socialization need not wait until every vaccination is complete. Exposure must be selected around the puppy's health, local disease risk and veterinary advice. Avoid sick animals and high-traffic dog areas of unknown health status. A puppy that is withdrawing or frightened needs a gentler plan, not forced participation. This is a planning module, not class-entry clearance or a vaccination schedule. ### Build an exposure map Create rows for household sounds, floor surfaces, grooming equipment, vehicles, calm people, distant animals and ordinary environments. Add columns for the specific experience, safe location, veterinary restrictions, starting distance, puppy response, recovery and next step. Mark each row **not introduced**, **comfortable**, **needs an easier version**, or **paused for advice**. These are worksheet labels, not developmental test scores. A long completed checklist is not the objective; comfortable experiences and recovery are. Before an outing, identify a retreat route and choose a quiet observation point. Ask the veterinarian which settings and contacts are appropriate now, given actual records and local outbreaks. Discuss safe alternatives when public ground exposure is unsuitable. Do not assume a carried puppy, vehicle or disinfected venue makes every exposure risk-free. Offer one manageable novelty rather than a crowded sequence. Let the puppy notice without requiring approach, greetings or a sit. Reward voluntary orientation or exploration at a comfortable distance. If interaction is offered, ensure the person can stop and let the puppy leave. Calm observation counts as success. Move away when avoidance, freezing or escalating excitement appears; do not keep moving closer until the puppy gives up. ### Training integration and review Practice a previously easy name response or hand target only when the puppy is comfortable. Separate exposure sessions from demanding duration work. Use YES only when a treat is available; GOOD is not a requirement to hold still through a frightening encounter. Schedule ordinary toilet access and protected rest rather than adding another exposure simply to fill a quota. **Record:** date, health restrictions, location, people/animals present, distance, voluntary choices, appetite for usual rewards, time to settle afterward and what will be easier next time. Food acceptance alone does not establish absence of fear. **Escalate:** illness signs, repeated avoidance, panic, inability to recover or unsafe interactions warrant veterinary advice and qualified behavior support. Do not wait for a checklist deadline. **Q: Must my puppy meet every dog?** No. Choose safe, comfortable experiences; neutral observation is useful. **Q: Did I miss the chance if the puppy is older?** Continue carefully tailored learning; do not attempt to compensate with overwhelming exposure.

records.body: # Supreme Canine Academy — Canine care and life-stage planning Private review draft • 2026-11-01 • General education, observation and veterinary referral support, not diagnosis, treatment or a validated clinical resource. Seven modules supplement the training and nutrition collections; they do not replace either. Original planning worksheets below are editorial proposals, not tested clinical instruments. Source identities and claim provenance are maintained separately. **Training language throughout:** YES ends the position and promises a treat; GOOD means remain in position with reward later; NO means stop unwanted behavior; NOPE means adjust an incorrect playful teaching attempt; OKAY is general release. Positional commands imply holding until release or another command. Pain, fear, illness, exhaustion and urgent care are not obedience failures. Never use this cue system to compel a distressed dog to tolerate care. ## EDU-000502 — Adolescence and apparent regression ### Purpose and evidence boundary Behavior can change with maturation, but age does not explain every new problem. Unexpected changes deserve assessment rather than a label such as stubbornness. Growing independence, environmental novelty and inconsistent learning histories can be considered in a training review; pain and illness must not be dismissed as adolescent behavior. ### Run a context audit Choose one concern, described observably: “responded to recall indoors but not near the fence,” rather than “has no respect.” Compare the current situation with the last successful version. List distance, distraction, duration, reward, equipment, access to competing activities, handler wording and household changes. Note whether the same difficulty occurs in a familiar quiet room. Keep management reliable while investigating. Use secure boundaries and suitable supervision rather than testing off-leash reliability in unsafe places. Prevent rehearsal of a problem without removing normal opportunities for rest, exploration, play and companionship. Agree on one cue and one response plan across caregivers; write down differences instead of blaming the dog for conflicting signals. Rebuild at an easier level: begin where the dog can succeed comfortably, give the familiar cue once, and reward the actual desired response. Reduce one challenge at a time. Keep a separate column for “not yet taught here” so lack of generalization is not recorded as deliberate refusal. Do not repeatedly issue a cue while the dog is too distracted to respond. End with an easy comfortable activity or ordinary rest, not a confrontation. ### Decision boundaries If performance is variable only in difficult contexts, revise the teaching setup and collect observations. If there is a sudden broad change, discomfort, sleep or elimination change, unexpected aggression or reduced willingness to move, arrange veterinary assessment. Bite risk or escalating fear also requires qualified behavior help. This module does not prescribe physical corrections, equipment escalation or a fixed age when behavior must resolve. **Record:** specific cue, location, challenge level, successful response count out of actual opportunities, recovery after distraction, and any physical/behavioral changes outside training. Count an opportunity only when the cue was actually presented under the planned conditions. **Q: Should I repeat all puppy training from scratch?** Revisit affected skills in easier contexts; retain what remains comfortable and reliable. **Q: Should I make GOOD mean a stronger stay?** No. Keep its meaning consistent: remain in position, reward later. Release with YES and a treat or OKAY as appropriate. A physically uncomfortable position is a reason to stop and investigate, not extend duration.

records.body: # Supreme Canine Academy — Canine care and life-stage planning Private review draft • 2026-11-01 • General education, observation and veterinary referral support, not diagnosis, treatment or a validated clinical resource. Seven modules supplement the training and nutrition collections; they do not replace either. Original planning worksheets below are editorial proposals, not tested clinical instruments. Source identities and claim provenance are maintained separately. **Training language throughout:** YES ends the position and promises a treat; GOOD means remain in position with reward later; NO means stop unwanted behavior; NOPE means adjust an incorrect playful teaching attempt; OKAY is general release. Positional commands imply holding until release or another command. Pain, fear, illness, exhaustion and urgent care are not obedience failures. Never use this cue system to compel a distressed dog to tolerate care. ## EDU-000503 — Exercise, enrichment and rest planning ### Purpose and evidence boundary Activity should suit the individual dog's health, development, mobility and environment. This guide does not prescribe minutes per month of age, mileage, jump heights or a universal sleep quota. Veterinary restrictions take priority. A dog repeatedly chasing a toy is not necessarily choosing a safe workload. ### Build a sustainable day Use a simple planner with columns for movement, exploration, learning, social contact and undisturbed rest. Record what actually happened rather than an ideal schedule. Include ordinary short activities: a comfortable sniffing opportunity, a familiar low-effort food puzzle when appropriate, a brief training game, or quiet time near a trusted person. Enrichment need not always involve food or high-intensity movement; feeding choices belong in the nutrition plan. Before choosing an activity, check footing, heat, shade, traffic, escape risk, available water and the dog's current condition. Ask the veterinarian about activity limits where there is illness, injury, a major fitness change or uncertainty about strenuous exercise. A previously athletic dog returning after inactivity should not automatically resume the old workload. Start with a comfortable familiar activity and observe before, during and afterward. Give genuine opportunities to stop. Alternate types of engagement rather than adding physical effort every time the dog appears busy. A rest space should be comfortable and protected from interruptions, not used as punishment. Teach settling separately from trying to exhaust the dog. ### Review the pattern Use a daily row: chosen activity; conditions; willingness to participate; movement; recovery; rest opportunity; next-day observation. Review whether the plan is achievable by all caregivers. If an activity cannot be offered safely, substitute an easier option rather than compressing missed exercise into a single demanding session. A practical experiment is to change one ordinary, low-risk scheduling element and observe the result. For example, move a quiet learning game away from a hectic household period. Do not run exercise experiments on a dog showing illness or pain. This planner is not a rehabilitation prescription or proof that exercise caused a behavioral improvement. **Stop/escalate:** limping, reluctance to continue, unusual breathing, weakness or distress mean stop the activity and obtain veterinary guidance; collapse or major breathing difficulty is an emergency. Do not demand a down-stay as a substitute for care. **Q: More exercise for every behavior problem?** No. Review environment, teaching, rest and health; fear and distress are not solved by fatigue. **Q: Does GOOD mean the dog cannot move while resting?** No. Ordinary rest is not an indefinite commanded position. Use cues only for deliberate, appropriate training moments.

records.body: # Supreme Canine Academy — Canine care and life-stage planning Private review draft • 2026-11-01 • General education, observation and veterinary referral support, not diagnosis, treatment or a validated clinical resource. Seven modules supplement the training and nutrition collections; they do not replace either. Original planning worksheets below are editorial proposals, not tested clinical instruments. Source identities and claim provenance are maintained separately. **Training language throughout:** YES ends the position and promises a treat; GOOD means remain in position with reward later; NO means stop unwanted behavior; NOPE means adjust an incorrect playful teaching attempt; OKAY is general release. Positional commands imply holding until release or another command. Pain, fear, illness, exhaustion and urgent care are not obedience failures. Never use this cue system to compel a distressed dog to tolerate care. ## EDU-000504 — Coat, skin, ears and mouth: observation before intervention ### Purpose and evidence boundary Routine grooming can reveal changes needing veterinary assessment. New itching, hair loss, redness, discharge or pain should be recorded rather than automatically treated as a training issue. Dental concerns include altered chewing, dropped food, mouth odor, swelling, bleeding or damaged teeth; a comfortable-looking exterior cannot rule out disease below the gumline. Brushing supports oral care but is not a substitute for veterinary dentistry. ### Make care predictable Keep a brief care card for each area: ordinary appearance, usual comfortable handling, approved tools/products, last professional advice and current concern. Use the cooperative-care training modules for gradual handling skills. This section does not duplicate their chin-rest, paw or brush teaching steps. Choose good light and nonslip footing; stop before the dog needs to struggle to escape. Observe without restraining a painful area. Note the location of changes on a simple body outline and take a photo only if safe. Record when the change was first noticed, whether it is spreading, and whether touching, eating or movement appears uncomfortable. Avoid declaring a cause from color, odor or an internet image. For ordinary brushing, use an appropriate tool and a comfortable amount of contact. Do not pull through tight mats against the skin or cut close to skin to avoid seeking help. Ask a qualified groomer or veterinarian which service is appropriate, especially if skin is sore. For ears, stay within the demonstration and product plan provided by the veterinary team; do not insert objects into the canal or improvise a cleaning mixture. This is not an ear-flushing or medication guide. Ask the veterinary team to demonstrate a comfortable home dental routine and suitable dog products. Do not use this module for scraping teeth, extracting loose teeth, forced mouth examinations or treating oral pain. If the dog resists care suddenly, pause and investigate rather than interpreting it as a failure of the cooperative-care cue. ### Documentation and questions **Record:** body area, date, appearance, comfort, changes in behavior, photos available, professional contacted and advice received. Maintain the original instructions for any prescribed treatment outside this training guide. **Q: Can I hold a GOOD position to finish quickly?** Not through pain or distress. Cooperative handling depends on comfort and a safe stopping plan. **Q: Should I clean an ear because it smells?** Ask the veterinary team; odor does not identify the cause or the appropriate treatment. **Q: Can training fix painful brushing?** Training cannot remove a painful medical or coat problem. Address that first.

records.body: # Supreme Canine Academy — Canine care and life-stage planning Private review draft • 2026-11-01 • General education, observation and veterinary referral support, not diagnosis, treatment or a validated clinical resource. Seven modules supplement the training and nutrition collections; they do not replace either. Original planning worksheets below are editorial proposals, not tested clinical instruments. Source identities and claim provenance are maintained separately. **Training language throughout:** YES ends the position and promises a treat; GOOD means remain in position with reward later; NO means stop unwanted behavior; NOPE means adjust an incorrect playful teaching attempt; OKAY is general release. Positional commands imply holding until release or another command. Pain, fear, illness, exhaustion and urgent care are not obedience failures. Never use this cue system to compel a distressed dog to tolerate care. ## EDU-000505 — Preventive visits, records and useful veterinary questions ### Purpose and evidence boundary Preventive plans are individualized. Vaccination decisions depend on history, exposure, lifestyle and applicable requirements; parasite testing and protection also depend on the dog and its risks. This module prepares a useful conversation, not a vaccine calendar or product prescription. Do not substitute old training material for current veterinary guidance. ### Prepare a one-page visit brief Begin with the dog's identification, usual clinic, relevant records and the three most important questions. Separate documented dates from estimates and unknowns. Bring prior vaccine certificates and laboratory reports when available; do not reconstruct an uncertain history as confirmed fact. Keep the exact names and instructions for current medications, preventives and supplements in the clinical record rather than anonymizing them. Add a concise lifestyle inventory: home setting, other animals, boarding/daycare, classes, travel destinations, outdoor access, wildlife exposure and planned changes. Describe any previous suspected vaccine or medication reaction accurately, including timing and what the veterinarian concluded. Do not call every later symptom a confirmed adverse reaction. Prepare behavior observations that may affect the visit: handling sensitivities, comfortable positions, reward preferences, escape concerns and bite history. Ask about waiting arrangements and whether any previsit plan is needed. Do not administer a calming drug suggested by this guide; it provides none. Discuss safe examination support with the veterinary team. ### Questions worth asking - Which preventive measures are recommended for this dog's actual circumstances, and why? - Which records are missing, and how should uncertain or overdue history be handled? - What changes in travel, household or activities should trigger a plan review? - Which parasite tests or protection are appropriate, and what should we do about missed doses? Do not double or restart products based on a chatbot answer. - What effects after care require an immediate call, and which number should we use after hours? - What should we record at home, and when is follow-up due? At the visit, note the decision, its reason, who gave the instruction and the follow-up date. Afterward, read back unclear instructions before leaving or contact the clinic. Put reminders in a calendar using the actual plan, not a generic schedule copied from the internet. Keep a separate “questions still unresolved” list. **Q: Can I skip a visit because the dog looks fine?** This guide cannot determine that; agree on preventive review timing with the veterinarian. **Q: Should source names be removed from medical records too?** No. Reader-facing training examples can be fictional; real clinical products, providers and records must remain accurate for safe care.

Source identities and claim provenance are maintained separately. **Training language throughout:** YES ends the position and promises a treat; GOOD means remain in position with reward later; NO means stop unwanted behavior; NOPE means adjust an incorrect playful teaching attempt; OKAY is general release. Positional commands imply holding until release or another command. Pain, fear, illness, exhaustion and urgent care are not obedience failures. Never use this cue system to compel a distressed dog to tolerate care. ## EDU-000505 — Preventive visits, records and useful veterinary questions ### Purpose and evidence boundary Preventive plans are individualized. Vaccination decisions depend on history, exposure, lifestyle and applicable requirements; parasite testing and protection also depend on the dog and its risks. This module prepares a useful conversation, not a vaccine calendar or product prescription. Do not substitute old training material for current veterinary guidance. ### Prepare a one-page visit brief Begin with the dog's identification, usual clinic, relevant records and the three most important questions. Separate documented dates from estimates and unknowns. Bring prior vaccine certificates and laboratory reports when available; do not reconstruct an uncertain history as confirmed fact. Keep the exact names and instructions for current medications, preventives and supplements in the clinical record rather than anonymizing them. Add a concise lifestyle inventory: home setting, other animals, boarding/daycare, classes, travel destinations, outdoor access, wildlife exposure and planned changes. Describe any previous suspected vaccine or medication reaction accurately, including timing and what the veterinarian concluded. Do not call every later symptom a confirmed adverse reaction. Prepare behavior observations that may affect the visit: handling sensitivities, comfortable positions, reward preferences, escape concerns and bite history. Ask about waiting arrangements and whether any previsit plan is needed. Do not administer a calming drug suggested by this guide; it provides none. Discuss safe examination support with the veterinary team. ### Questions worth asking - Which preventive measures are recommended for this dog's actual circumstances, and why? - Which records are missing, and how should uncertain or overdue history be handled? - What changes in travel, household or activities should trigger a plan review? - Which parasite tests or protection are appropriate, and what should we do about missed doses? Do not double or restart products based on a chatbot answer. - What effects after care require an immediate call, and which number should we use after hours? - What should we record at home, and when is follow-up due? At the visit, note the decision, its reason, who gave the instruction and the follow-up date. Afterward, read back unclear instructions before leaving or contact the clinic. Put reminders in a calendar using the actual plan, not a generic schedule copied from the internet. Keep a separate “questions still unresolved” list. **Q: Can I skip a visit because the dog looks fine?** This guide cannot determine that; agree on preventive review timing with the veterinarian. **Q: Should source names be removed from medical records too?** No. Reader-facing training examples can be fictional; real clinical products, providers and records must remain accurate for safe care.

records.title: Senior comfort, accessibility and changed behavior
records.summary: See module decision boundaries; pain, illness or distress supersedes obedience. Emergency list is not exhaustive.
records.body: # Supreme Canine Academy — Canine care and life-stage planning Private review draft • 2026-11-01 • General education, observation and veterinary referral support, not diagnosis, treatment or a validated clinical resource. Seven modules supplement the training and nutrition collections; they do not replace either. Original planning worksheets below are editorial proposals, not tested clinical instruments. Source identities and claim provenance are maintained separately. **Training language throughout:** YES ends the position and promises a treat; GOOD means remain in position with reward later; NO means stop unwanted behavior; NOPE means adjust an incorrect playful teaching attempt; OKAY is general release. Positional commands imply holding until release or another command. Pain, fear, illness, exhaustion and urgent care are not obedience failures. Never use this cue system to compel a distressed dog to tolerate care. ## EDU-000506 — Senior comfort, accessibility and changed behavior ### Purpose and evidence boundary Senior care includes physical comfort, mobility, sensory changes, behavior and quality of life. Changes such as disorientation, disrupted sleep, altered social interaction, house-soiling or new anxiety need assessment; they are not automatically dementia or inevitable aging. Keep a history of eating, drinking, movement and elimination for the veterinary team. ### Build an accessibility map Walk through the dog's ordinary routes: bed to water, resting area to outside, vehicle access and favorite family spaces. List slippery surfaces, obstacles, steps, tight turns and places where the dog may become stuck. Choose stable, low-risk changes such as clearing routes, improving traction and keeping essential items accessible. Ask for professional guidance on ramps, lifting aids or mobility equipment rather than assuming any device fits safely. Keep the layout predictable when the dog depends on familiar routes. Provide a comfortable resting location where people will not repeatedly disturb the dog. Plan toilet access around the individual pattern rather than demanding that an older dog maintain a former interval. Consider how each caregiver will implement the same arrangements when the primary person is absent. ### Adapt learning without withdrawing companionship Retain easy, enjoyable activities that the dog can perform comfortably. Shorten or simplify a task when needed; do not force repeated sit-down transitions to prove the dog remembers. Allow a comfortable alternative to a position that appears difficult. If hearing or vision changes are suspected, seek assessment and discuss appropriate cue adaptations. Do not startle-test the dog or punish a missed signal. Create a small “ordinary pleasures” list: greeting a familiar person, resting nearby, comfortable exploration or a favored gentle activity. Record access and apparent enjoyment without turning the list into a numerical diagnosis or an automatic end-of-life decision. Quality-of-life decisions require the caregiver and veterinary team, with the dog's individual circumstances central. ### Record and escalate Use a daily change log when concerns arise: time, context, observable event, duration, recovery, and effect on eating, rest or movement. Videos can help if taken without provoking or delaying care. Bring the trend, not just the worst moment, to the veterinarian. Sudden severe confusion, collapse, major breathing difficulty or other emergency signs belong in urgent care, not a routine review queue. **Q: Is a forgotten cue proof of cognitive decline?** No. Hearing, vision, discomfort, context and other causes require consideration. **Q: Should I correct new indoor accidents?** No. Review access and obtain veterinary assessment. **Q: Is GOOD appropriate for a painful posture?** No; release the training demand and address comfort.
